title: Spatial Clustering of Termites but Not Fungi at Site‐Scale Drive Global Wood Decay Patterns
content:
Termites and fungi predominantly drive global deadwood decomposition. However, it remains unknown if they affect site-scale wood decomposition via forming emergent spatial patterns. This study highlights that termites and fungi, when highly abundant, form clustered and overdispersed spatial patterns, respectively, enhancing and lowering site-scale deadwood decomposition. Notably, the human footprint more strongly suppresses termite clustering than climate and thus decelerates wood decomposition, which neutralizes the accelerating effects of favorable climate conditions and adds uncertainty to the fate of deadwood carbon pools.


ABSTRACT

Deadwood stores ~8% of global forest carbon, and termites and fungi are its primary decomposers—organisms whose activities are likely to intensify under global warming. Yet it remains unclear how their site-scale spatial self-organization—whether clustered or overdispersed—varies with global change stressors and shapes global wood decomposition patterns. Leveraging a global experiment, we find that increasing termite spatial occupancy is associated with more clustered patterns of decomposition rates, whereas higher fungal spatial occupancy is associated with more overdispersed patterns. Notably, temperature more strongly increases termite occupancy and thus indirectly contributes to clustered patterns, while anthropogenic pressure more strongly and directly promotes overdispersed patterns by reducing termite occupancy. Termite-driven clustering is positively associated with site-scale decomposition rates, contributing as much to global variation as termite occupancy and temperature. In contrast, fungi-driven overdispersion slightly decelerates site-scale decomposition rates via weakening the positive effects of fungal occupancy. Our study highlights that the within-site spatial patterns of decomposer activities are important drivers of global wood decomposition. Under global warming, termite clustering and range expansion may contribute to accelerating deadwood decomposition. However, human disturbances slow decomposition by disrupting termites' self-organization, adding uncertainty to the fate of deadwood carbon pools.

摘要

木质残体储存了全球森林约8%的碳储量，而白蚁和真菌正是其主要的分解者。这两种生物类群的分解活动在全球变暖背景下可能会不断增强。然而，当前研究尚未探明两种分解者类群在样地尺度上的空间自组织模式(聚集型vs.过度分散型)如何随全球变化因子发生变化，并最终塑造木材分解速率的全球格局。基于一项已公开发表的全球木质残体分解实验数据集，我们发现白蚁空间占有率的增加与分解速率的聚集型模式正相关，而真菌空间占有率的增加则与过度分散型模式正相关。值得注意的是，温度上升会更强烈地增加白蚁空间占有率，从而间接促进分解速率的聚集模式；而人类活动压力则通过降低白蚁空间占有率，更强烈且直接地促进分解速率的过度分散模式。进一步分析表明，由白蚁驱动的聚集模式与样地尺度的分解速率均值呈正相关，其对分解速率全球变异性的贡献程度与白蚁空间占有率和温度相当。相比之下，由真菌驱动的过度分散模式则通过削弱真菌空间占有率的促进作用，对样地尺度的分解速率均值产生较为微弱的负效应。本研究揭示了分解者活动在样地尺度的空间自组织模式是全球木材分解的重要驱动因素。在全球变暖背景下，白蚁的聚集模式及其空间分布范围的扩张可能进一步加快木质残体分解。然而，人类活动会改变白蚁的空间自组织模式进而抑制木质残体的分解速率，为全球变化背景下预测木质残体碳库的动态增添了不确定性。
